## Proposition 9.12
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit will also be measured by the same.

**Step 1.** Let 1, A, B, C, ..., D, E be as many numbers as we please beginning from a unit in continued proportion, and let E (the last) be measured by some prime number p.

**Step 2.** Since the numbers 1, A, B, C, ..., D, E are in continued proportion, consecutive terms satisfy the same ratio: 1:A = A:B = B:C = ... = D:E [by D7.20, definition of proportional numbers].

**Step 3.** Consider the last pair in the proportion: 1:A = D:E. Since these four numbers are proportional, by Proposition 7.19, the product of the extremes equals the product of the means: 1 times E equals A times D, that is, E = A times D.

**Step 4.** Since p is prime and p measures E, and E = A times D, the prime p measures the product of A and D. By Proposition 7.30, if a prime number measures the product of two numbers, it must measure one of them. Therefore p measures A or p measures D.

**Step 5.** If p measures A, then the next to the unit is measured by p, which is what was to be proved.

**Step 6.** Suppose instead that p measures D. Consider the preceding pair in the proportion: 1:A = C:D (where C is the term before D). By the same reasoning as Step 3, applying 7.19, we get D = A times C. Since p measures D and D = A times C, by 7.30, p measures A or p measures C.

**Step 7.** If p measures A, we are done. If p measures C, we repeat the argument: from 1:A = (term before C):C, we obtain C = A times (term before C), and again by 7.30, p measures A or p measures the term before C.

**Step 8.** Continuing in this manner, we descend through the sequence term by term. At each stage, either p measures A (and we are done) or p measures the preceding term, and we apply the same argument again. Since the sequence is finite and begins from the unit, this descent must eventually reach the term A itself.

**Step 9.** When we reach A: from the proportion 1:A = A:B, we have B = A times A by 7.19. If we arrived here because p measures B, then since B = A times A, by 7.30, p measures A.

**Step 10.** Therefore, in all cases, p measures A. Since this holds for any prime p that measures the last term E, we conclude: by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit will also be measured by the same. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 7.19, 7.30, D7.11, D7.20
**Human refs (from References field):** 7.19, 7.20, 7.21, 7.29, 9.11, 9.8, D7.14

heath_proof_text: Let there be as many numbers as we please, A, B, C, D, beginning from an unit, and in continued proportion; I say that, by however many prime numbers D is measured, A will also be measured by the same. For let D be measured by any prime number E; I say that E measures A. For suppose it does not; now E is prime, and any prime number is prime to any which it does not measure; [VII. 29] therefore E, A are prime to one another. And, since E measures D, let it measure it according to F, therefore E by multiplying F has made D. Again, since A measures D according to the units in C, [IX. 11 and Por.] therefore A by multiplying C has made D. But, further, E has also by multiplying F made D; therefore the product of A, C is equal to the product of E, F. Therefore, as A is to E, so is F to C. [VII. 19] But A, E are prime, primes are also least, [VII. 21] and the least measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent; [VII. 20] therefore E measures C. Let it measure it according to G; therefore E by multiplying G has made C. But, further, by the theorem before this, A has also by multiplying B made C. [IX. 11 and Por.] Therefore the product of A, B is equal to the product of E, G. Therefore, as A is to E, so is G to B. [VII. 19] But A, E are prime, primes are also least, [VII. 21] and the least numbers measure those which have the same ratio with them the same number of times, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent: [VII. 20] therefore E measures B. Let it measure it according to H; therefore E by multiplying H has made B. But further A has also by multiplying itself made B; [IX. 8] therefore the product of E, H is equal to the square on A. Therefore, as E is to A, so is A to H. [VII. 19] But A, E are prime, primes are also least, [VII. 21] and the least measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent; [VII. 20] therefore E measures A, as antecedent antecedent. But, again, it also does not measure it: which is impossible. Therefore E, A are not prime to one another. Therefore they are composite to one another. But numbers composite to one another are measured by some number. [VII. Def. 14] And, since E is by hypothesis prime, and the prime is not measured by any number other than itself, therefore E measures A, E, so that E measures A. [But it also measures D; therefore E measures A, D.] Similarly we can prove that, by however many prime numbers D is measured, A will also be measured by the same.
